question.text:
You are analyzing the performance of two equity funds over the past five years. Here are the annual returns: Fund X: 8%, 12%, -5%, 15%, 10% Fund Y: 10%, 9%, -3%, 18%, 8%
Compute the Sharpe Ratio for Fund X assuming a risk-free rate of 3%.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the workbook, Sharpe Ratio = (Average Return − Risk-Free Rate) / Standard Deviation of Returns. Fund X average = (8 + 12 − 5 + 15 + 10) / 5 = 8%. The sample standard deviation of Fund X's returns is √(238/4) ≈ 7.71%. Sharpe = (8% − 3%) / 7.71% ≈ 0.65. The Trap: 0.75 tempts candidates who mis-state the denominator as 6.67%. 0.82 tempts those who use population standard deviation (dividing by n). 0.91 tempts those who forget to subtract the risk-free rate from the numerator. Note: Use sample standard deviation (divide by n−1) consistent with the workbook formula; if population standard deviation were used the result would be ≈ 0.72, which is not among the listed options.
